sources.title: Two Common Mistakes On The Volley | Tennis Volley Technique
Ultimate Tennis Volley Guide | Fix Mistakes With Simple Drills!
ATP Coach Exposes My Volley Mistakes (and How He Fixed Them)
Common Mistakes to Avoid on the Volley - Pro Tennis Tips with Coach Rhett
2 Mistakes To Avoid To DOMINATE At The Net - Volley Tennis Lesson
5 Reasons Why You’re Missing Tennis Volleys & How To Fix The Mistakes
Your Volley Technique Is Wrong—Here's Why
Fixing the Most Common Volley Mistake | Backhand Volley Lesson with Diana
The Most Common Errors On The Volley And How To Fix Them
Avoid These 3 Common Volley & Overhead Mistakes (Singles Strategy Explained)
Volley Technique That Actually Works | No More Mistakes

good_form: Use only a minimal body turn on the volley, just enough to hit the ball out to the side of the body.
On the forehand volley, turn only a small amount; never turn all the way as you would on a groundstroke.
The backhand volley turn can be slightly larger than on the forehand, but it should still be small.
Keep the hand and elbow in front of the body.
You can lag the racket head behind slightly for extra power while the hand stays in front.
Use a ready position with a comfortable knee bend and the upper body tilted slightly down in a sprinter stance, with the body in a slight C shape.
The sprinter stance keeps the elbows comfortably in front so they are unlikely to tuck in.

faults.name: Excessive body turn
faults.looks_like: Turning the body fully, as on a groundstroke, on the forehand or backhand volley, so the hand and elbow end up far behind the body.
faults.why_it_matters: The big turn leads to a big arm swing, which makes the volley hard to control.
causes: Turning the body as if hitting a groundstroke
A big turn that puts the hand and elbow too far behind the body
fixes: Keep the turn minimal, just enough to meet the ball outside the body
Keep the hand and elbow in front of the body
Lag the racket head behind slightly if you want extra power
outcome_effects: The swing is too large with the whole arm
The volley is hard to control

faults.name: Tucked-in elbow
faults.looks_like: On the forehand volley, the elbow gets tucked in and pulled back behind the body.
faults.why_it_matters: The volley then depends heavily on forearm and wrist movement, since you are almost forced to swing with the wrist and forearm.
causes: Not having a proper ready position
Relying on knee bend alone, since squatting down can still leave the elbows tucked in
Not tilting the upper body down into the sprinter stance
fixes: Take a comfortable knee bend and lean the upper body slightly down into the sprinter stance, in a slight C shape
Drill: hold a broomstick under the elbows so they cannot go back, and volley like that for about five minutes
With the broomstick in place, lag the racket tip behind to get power before contact
outcome_effects: Swinging with the wrist and forearm
With the broomstick drill: immediate improvement in control, crisper volleys, better contact, and more power

good_form: Treat the volley as a pushing or stepping motion, not a groundstroke swing.
Keep the volley compact, efficient and fast, like a short punch.
Start in a ready position with elbows and armpits aired out, not elbows down.
Hold the racket at about a 45 degree angle in the ready position.
Bend the knees slightly and stay on your toes.
Use a split step before moving into the forehand or backhand volley.
Do a unit turn, then step into the ball with the front foot while pushing off the back leg.
Think of it as three beats: ready position, turn, push or step.
Use the composite grip at bevel 2.5, between the continental (bevel 2) and bevel 3, for leverage and racket position.
Keep the racket face flat, like a wall, at contact.
Be intense and quick, because the volley is largely a reaction shot.
Hold the finish position after contact to check follow-through and feel.
Positioning is crucial on the volley.

faults.name: Swinging at the volley
faults.looks_like: Taking a big groundstroke-style swing at the ball instead of a short push or punch.
faults.why_it_matters: The speaker says swinging at the volley always leads to a mistake. The volley should stay compact, efficient and fast.
causes: Treating the volley like a groundstroke
fixes: Think of the volley as a push or a step.
Keep the swing path very compact, like a punch.
Practice the palm-the-ball drill, the fence drill, shadow swings and drop-feed volleys with a held finish.
outcome_effects: Errors, such as hitting the ball out

faults.name: Elbows down in ready position
faults.looks_like: Standing in the ready position with the elbows tucked down instead of aired out.
faults.why_it_matters: The speaker presents airing the elbows and armpits as part of a correct ready position.
fixes: Air the elbows and armpits.
Hold the racket at 45 degrees, with knees slightly bent and weight on the toes.

good_form: Stand very tight to the net, less than a foot from the net strap, so you are already there and have no time to close.
Don't split step when that close; keep the feet active instead.
Move through the ball to keep body weight going forward, so even a mis-hit still clears the net.
Treat the volley as a block with no swing, as if protecting yourself with a shield.
Close to the ball square and forward, using linear momentum through it.
A two-handed backhand volley is acceptable for balls above the shoulders or coming with a lot of speed.
When the ball comes straight at your chest, take it on the backhand side, since that is easier than moving the feet for a forehand.

faults.name: Not closing forward through the volley
faults.looks_like: Not moving forward into the ball, so the volley pops up.
faults.why_it_matters: Without forward movement the ball pops up instead of being put away or placed back deep.
causes: Not closing square and forward with linear momentum through the ball
fixes: Close more square and forward, moving linearly through the ball to keep weight forward

faults.name: Taking a chest-high ball on the forehand
faults.looks_like: Hitting a ball coming right at the chest with the forehand volley, which forces lots of foot movement.
faults.why_it_matters: The extra footwork can leave you out of position.
causes: Ball coming directly at the chest or midsection at speed
fixes: Take it on the backhand side instead, as it is easier

faults.name: Splitting when right on top of the net
faults.looks_like: Trying to split step when already less than a foot from the net.
faults.why_it_matters: There is no time to split when so close, so you can't react in time.
causes: Being very tight to the net
fixes: Skip the split, keep the feet active, and move through the ball

good_form: Pretend your back is up against a wall so the racket can't go back at all.
Keep the racket in front and treat the volley like a simple catch, like a first baseman catching a throw.
Keep the wrist firm and don't let it collapse or break.
Watch the ball, not your target or your opponent.
Think: no swing, no butt cap showing, no wrist collapse.

faults.name: Taking the racket back
faults.looks_like: Taking the racket back so the opponent can see the butt cap, then launching at the ball.
faults.why_it_matters: It turns the volley into a swing instead of a simple catch-like contact.
causes: Not treating the volley as a catch; taking a swing-style backswing
fixes: Pretend you're up against a wall so the racket can't go back
Think of it as a catch, with no swing and no butt cap shown
outcome_effects: The ball typically goes out because the racket face is angled up at contact

faults.name: Wrist break
faults.looks_like: The wrist collapses or breaks at contact.
faults.why_it_matters: It changes the racket face angle at contact and sends the ball down.
fixes: Keep the wrist firm with no collapse; just catch the volley
outcome_effects: The racket face goes down and the ball goes into the net

faults.name: Not watching the ball
faults.looks_like: Looking at the target or the opponent instead of the ball.
faults.why_it_matters: It stops you from hitting the volley cleanly.
causes: Focusing on the target or the opponent
fixes: Watch the ball, like catching it
Don't watch the target or the opponent

good_form: Imagine the racket head and the net are magnetized, so at the end of the volley the net seems to pull the racket toward it.
Finish the volley with good extension toward the net.
Keep the grip looser instead of squeezing it hard.
The magnetized feel lets you release the racket into the volley, giving a cleaner, deeper volley.
For a deliberate short volley, keep the same magnetized feel and loosen the grip further so the shortness is chosen, not forced.
The feel applies to both forehand and backhand volleys.

faults.name: Dumping the volley short
faults.looks_like: The volley finish is abrupt, the arm stays bent, and the grip is squeezed too tightly, so the arm feels heavy.
faults.why_it_matters: The ball sits down short, usually before the service line, which gives the opponent an easy time with the volley. It tends to happen under pressure when the shot feels important.
causes: Abrupt finish to the volley
Arm stays bent with limited extension
Grip squeezed too tight, so the player arm-wrestles the ball and the arm feels heavy
Pressure when the shot feels like it matters
fixes: Imagine the racket head and net are magnetized, so the net pulls the racket toward it at the end of the volley
Extend the arm toward the net
Loosen the grip instead of squeezing
Release the racket into the volley
outcome_effects: Volley lands short, before the service line, when a deep one was wanted
Opponent gets an easy next shot

good_form: After an approach shot, move forward along the path of your ball, as if tethered or bungeed to it.
Following the ball lets you cut off angles and close the volley into open court.
Most of the time, approach down the line, because it shrinks the court and takes time and angles away.
Approaching cross court is reasonable when the opponent is pulled out into a corner or out of position.
After hitting deep, watch your opponent for visual cues about what they will hit.
Lob cue: the opponent is preparing to hit up and over you.
Drive cue: the opponent pulls the racket back and steps into the ball.
Topspin lob cue: the weight shifts to the back foot and the front foot lifts as they hit up.

faults.name: Not following your approach ball
faults.looks_like: Hitting an approach cross court and then moving forward without shifting to cover the ball's path, deviating from its line.
faults.why_it_matters: It leaves open court so the opponent can easily hit past you, which makes the net feel scary and unproductive.
causes: Deviating from the path of the ball you just struck
Not shifting over to cover the line after an approach cross court
fixes: Pretend you are tethered or bungeed to your ball and follow its path
Shift to cover as you move in so you can close the volley into open court
Approach down the line most of the time; go cross court mainly when the opponent is out of position
outcome_effects: The opponent hits a pass down the line past you
Open court angles are left available

faults.name: Ignoring the opponent's visual cues
faults.looks_like: Coming forward after the approach without watching whether the opponent is setting up to drive or lob.
faults.why_it_matters: You are not ready for what happens next. The speakers compare reading cues to making smart bets.
causes: Not paying attention to what the opponent is doing after your deep ball
Not recognizing the signs of a lob versus a drive
fixes: Look at your opponent after you hit deep
Read the lob cue versus the drive cue (racket back and stepping into the ball means drive)
For a topspin lob, watch for weight moving to the back foot and the front foot lifting
outcome_effects: Being unprepared for the opponent's shot

good_form: On higher, slower balls you can take a bit of a swing, but keep your legs under your upper body so you don't lean over the ball.
The lower and harder the ball, the shorter and sweeter the swing should be.
Set up with the racket tip pointing to the outside/side, leading with the lower edge of the racket.
Open the racket face more on low volleys and close it a little on higher balls near the net.
Split step, then step with the outside leg (the leg behind the side you're hitting on) behind the ball and stride forward from it; rhythm is hop, one, two.
If you have to move farther after the split step, use split, move, move, one-two, with a wider outside-leg step behind the ball and drive forward off that back leg.
Use the Continental grip for all volleys: index-finger underside and meaty palm base on bevel number two.
Start simple by choking up on the grip for more control, and shadow with the upper body set so you can stride toward your target.
Punch straight forward by extending the elbow to get pop, rather than swinging.
Hit down only on higher balls near the net; low volleys often need an upward motion to lift the ball. Adjust to the ball you get.

faults.name: Taking the racket back on hard, low balls
faults.looks_like: Taking a backswing when a hard, low ball is coming at you.
faults.why_it_matters: You will hit the ball late.
causes: Swinging on a ball that is coming harder and lower
fixes: Keep the swing short and sweet on lower, harder balls
Swing a little only on higher, slower balls

faults.name: Leaning over the ball when swinging
faults.looks_like: Upper body leans over the ball because the legs are not under it.
faults.why_it_matters: The speaker says you definitely don't want to lean over the ball.
causes: Swinging through without keeping the legs under the upper body
fixes: Keep your legs under your upper body as you move through the ball

faults.name: Racket tip pointing up
faults.looks_like: Racket tip points up to the sky (or straight ahead) when setting up for the volley.
faults.why_it_matters: You can't control the racket face angle or get under the ball.
fixes: Point the tip of the racket to the side
Lead with the lower edge of the racket
Open the face more on low volleys and close it slightly on high ones

faults.name: Wrong or no footwork (one step or cross step)
faults.looks_like: Taking one step, or one big cross step that pulls you sideways, instead of moving forward to the ball.
faults.why_it_matters: You want to put the ball over the net in front of you, and forward movement is how you get pop.
causes: Lessons feed the ball right to the player so one step is enough
Coaches' cross-step cue is misleading, so players take one big sideways step
fixes: Split step, set the outside foot behind the ball, then stride forward
Use a hop, one, two rhythm
When moving farther, split, move, move, one-two with a wide outside-leg step
Move laterally only when stretched wide

faults.name: Using a forehand grip (Eastern) on volleys
faults.looks_like: Hitting volleys, especially backhand ones, with a forehand grip or switching between Eastern grips.
faults.why_it_matters: It limits you, hurts the wrist at some point, and costs control.
causes: Advice to switch between Eastern forehand and backhand grips
Club players struggling even with one regular grip
fixes: Use the Continental grip for all volleys: index-finger underside and palm base on bevel two
outcome_effects: Nothing on the ball on the backhand
Ball pops up or goes into the net

faults.name: Chopping down on the volley
faults.looks_like: A karate-chop high-to-low motion down on the ball.
faults.why_it_matters: You get nothing on the ball, and too much rotation stops it going where you want.
causes: Taking the high-to-low coaching cue literally
fixes: Set up behind the ball and punch straight forward, extending the elbow
Hit down only on higher balls near the net, without chopping
Lift upward on low volleys
outcome_effects: Racket face opens and the ball pops up
Ball has too much rotation and lacks penetration

good_form: Use a continental (service) grip for forehand volley, backhand volley and overhead, with no grip change.
Continental grip makes low volleys easy because the racket face stays open.
Keep the elbow in front of you, slightly closer to the chest, on the forehand volley, squeezing the pecs a little.
On the backhand volley keep the non-hitting (left) elbow in front, turn the shoulders and keep the racket and elbow steady, with the left hand going behind you as you hit.
Hold the ready position with hands in front of you at belly-button height, racket angled between flat and vertical, then sit lower for low balls.
Make contact before the front foot lands: the foot is up at contact and the heel touches down in the follow-through.
Use the legs and body for pace and disguise; if you step in early and wait, drive forward with the back leg through the hit.
Direct the volley crosscourt or down the line by extending in that direction.
Set the strings to the ball as soon as you see it, steering the racket with the non-dominant hand holding it.
Start low with the racket in front, since most balls arrive around that height.

faults.name: Forehand grip on volleys
faults.looks_like: Holding a forehand grip when volleying on forehand and backhand sides and on low balls.
faults.why_it_matters: It makes forehand volleys hard to handle and forces wrist use; it is hard to get really good with this grip.
causes: Not having learned the continental grip first
fixes: Learn the continental grip first: thumb and index finger on the way down, high index finger.
Use it for forehand volley, backhand volley and overhead without changing.
Only experiment with small grip changes when advanced, play a lot of doubles and already volley well.
outcome_effects: Racket angle is open on low volleys, making them awkward

faults.name: Swing too big
faults.looks_like: Taking a large swing with the elbow moving back on the forehand, or the left elbow moving backward on the backhand.
faults.why_it_matters: A big swing makes volleys difficult; coaches say to block, but it is hard without knowing how.
causes: Elbow drifting back behind the body
On the backhand, the left elbow moving backward
fixes: Keep the forehand elbow in front and slightly toward the chest, squeezing the pecs.
On the backhand keep the left elbow in front.
Drill: a partner feeds and you catch the ball with the racket held in front, then volley with the left hand going behind you.
Turn the shoulders without moving racket or elbow.

faults.name: Racket dropping from hitting too far in front
faults.looks_like: The racket head goes down on contact and feels wobbly.
faults.why_it_matters: It makes deep volleys hard and gives no power.
causes: Contact too far in front of the body, so you cannot extend further
fixes: Keep hands in front at belly-button height as the starting position, racket between flat and vertical.
Sit lower to take balls at different heights.

faults.name: Wrong rhythm and timing with footwork
faults.looks_like: Stepping in, stopping, then hitting after the foot is down, standing up and just hitting without using the body.
faults.why_it_matters: Volleys rely on the legs for pace and disguise; without the body it is hard to control the ball.
causes: Being told to step in and hit the volley, so players step and then hit as separate actions
fixes: Practice the rhythm: contact while the foot is still up, then heel touches the ground in the follow-through, on both sides.
If you step in early and wait, hit while moving forward with the back leg.
Use the legs to direct the ball crosscourt or down the line.

faults.name: Racket starting too low and not setting strings early
faults.looks_like: Racket starts low, then has to go up to hit with a big swing, flailing around.
faults.why_it_matters: On fast balls there is no time to go from low to set up the strings.
causes: Racket starting too low
Not having the strings set as soon as the ball is seen
Mostly seen among beginners and players without coaches
fixes: Start in the ready position with racket in front and sit low.
Set the strings as soon as you see the ball.
Hold the racket throat with the non-dominant hand to steer the strings.

good_form: Use a continental grip for the backhand volley and keep the same grip.
Keep the wrist locked and the racket close to your body.
Wait for the ball to come to you instead of going out to find it.
Use your body to punch together with the racket, and let the racket punch off the ball.
Rotate your shoulders and body on the preparation.
Keep both hands on the racket (backhand) until the last second, then open and punch aggressively.
Stay a little away from the ball so you have space.
Look forward and down at the ball; don't turn to the side.
Keep the swing short and the contact solid, with a pop instead of a swing.
Keep the preparation small, because a big preparation leads to swinging and you can't punch.
Lean forward and finish low and in front.
Keep the arm a little bent when hitting rather than extended.
When switching between forehand and backhand, freeze the racket at contact and keep it simple.

faults.name: Bending the wrist / going out to find the ball
faults.looks_like: The wrist bends and the racket reaches far out in front to meet the ball.
faults.why_it_matters: The body is not connected to the shot, so the volley isn't solid.
causes: Not keeping the wrist locked
Going to find the ball instead of waiting for it
Not using the body to punch
fixes: Lock the wrist and keep the racket closer to the body
Wait for the ball to arrive
Use the body to punch with the racket
outcome_effects: Body is not with the shot

faults.name: Swinging at the volley
faults.looks_like: Taking a swing at the ball instead of a short punch.
faults.why_it_matters: Swinging loses power, whereas a short solid punch is more effective.
causes: Preparing big
Not staying solid at contact
fixes: Make the swing short and the contact solid with a pop
Keep the preparation small
Freeze the racket at contact
Just place the racket there and let the ball come back
Rotate the body instead of swinging

faults.name: Splitting the hands too early
faults.looks_like: The two hands separate early on the backhand preparation.
faults.why_it_matters: The arms are less solid, and the punch is less aggressive.
causes: Opening the arms before the last second
fixes: Rotate and wait with both hands on the racket
Open at the last second to punch aggressively
Let go to punch, not just to play the ball

faults.name: Moving too close to the ball
faults.looks_like: Stepping into the ball so it is too near the body.
faults.why_it_matters: You have no space to hit.
causes: Moving toward the ball
fixes: Stay a little away from the ball and let it come to you

faults.name: Turning the head to the side
faults.looks_like: Going to the side when hitting instead of looking forward.
faults.why_it_matters: The speaker doesn't want this; the gaze should stay forward and down.
fixes: Look forward and down at the ball

faults.name: Preparing big
faults.looks_like: A large backswing preparation.
faults.why_it_matters: With a big preparation you will swing and cannot punch.
fixes: Keep the preparation small; practice quick-fire balls so there is no time to swing

faults.name: Overextending the arm
faults.looks_like: The arm is extended out in front so you reach too much.
faults.why_it_matters: Extending is only for reaching a ball that is too far; otherwise it makes you reach.
causes: Arm extended in front
fixes: Bend the arm a little more when hitting
Hit with the arm bent

faults.name: Going down too much
faults.looks_like: Dropping down too far on the shot.
faults.why_it_matters: The speaker wants a simple, controlled volley.
fixes: Keep it simple and freeze the racket

good_form: Volley with the Continental grip so both the forehand and backhand sides of the racket can be used.
Keep the hands below the racket head so you can get under low balls.
Turn sideways like a groundstroke so you hit on the outside of the body, with a modest turn and small backswing.
Keep the elbow in front, in line with the outside foot, and set the racket to the side at about a 45° line.
Set the racket directly behind the ball and use the big muscles rather than a big arm swing.
Think of catching the ball on the strings; the racket lags slightly behind the hand while the hand stays in front and the hands stay close together.
Lead with the bottom edge of the racket so you can open the face, add a little slice for control and keep the ball low.
Volley with the feet: step out and in with weight transfer and momentum through the ball.
Load the outside foot first, so the last step before contact is with the foot on the same side as the ball, with the inside foot in the air as you move through the ball.
Practice from further back near the service line, with transitional volleys, rather than always right at the net.

faults.name: Wrong grip (Eastern forehand or Western)
faults.looks_like: Volleying with an Eastern forehand or more Western grip, using the same racket face on both sides of the body like a windscreen wiper.
faults.why_it_matters: It only works for high balls close to the net; on low balls you can't keep the hands below the racket head or use both racket faces.
causes: Habitually using a forehand grip rather than Continental
fixes: Use the Continental grip for volleys
outcome_effects: Players try to hit up with topspin on low balls
Poor racket-face control pops the ball straight up

faults.name: Too open body with racket straight up
faults.looks_like: Facing the net with the body open and the racket held straight up, instead of turning sideways.
faults.why_it_matters: The ball can only be hit downward and it is hard to get under it.
causes: Getting used to the forehand grip
fixes: Turn sideways like a groundstroke to hit on the outside of the body
Keep the turn modest and the backswing small
Keep the elbow in front in line with the outside foot and set the racket to the side at about 45°
outcome_effects: Struggle to get under the ball

faults.name: Weak wrist on the forehand volley
faults.looks_like: Not setting the racket to the side at roughly 45° on the forehand volley with a Continental grip.
faults.why_it_matters: It puts the wrist into a weak, uncomfortable position, which is why players often find the backhand volley more natural.
causes: Racket not set to the side on a 45° line
fixes: Set the racket to the side around a 45° line

faults.name: Too big a swing / punching or chopping
faults.looks_like: A big arm swing, with the racket not set directly behind the ball and the big muscles not used, so the player punches or chops at the ball with an abrupt, jerky motion.
faults.why_it_matters: It leaves no touch or feel.
causes: Lack of, or incorrect, footwork, not volleying with the feet
Not setting the racket behind the ball using the big muscles
fixes: Think of catching the ball on the strings
Let the racket lag slightly behind the hand and keep the hands close together
Lead with the bottom edge of the racket
Step out and in, loading the outside foot first, with weight transfer through the ball
outcome_effects: Ball doesn't stay low or controlled

faults.name: Overactive wrist
faults.looks_like: The racket overtakes the hand on the way through.
faults.why_it_matters: It makes the ball go crooked.
fixes: Keep the hand in front with the racket lagging slightly behind
Keep the hands close together

faults.name: Incorrect footwork (stepping across and stamping)
faults.looks_like: Not stepping out and in with the feet, or stepping across with one step and stamping as old advice says.
faults.why_it_matters: You lose the weight transfer and momentum through the ball, which leads to over-swinging.
causes: Old-school advice such as 'step across and punch'
Practicing only close to the net where footwork seems unnecessary
fixes: Load the outside foot first, with the last step on the same side as the ball
Have the inside foot in the air as you move through the ball, not just to it
outcome_effects: No weight transfer or momentum through the ball

faults.name: Practicing only very close to the net
faults.looks_like: Always setting up right at the net, using only one type of volley with the racket straight up, punching and with poor footwork.
faults.why_it_matters: It builds errors, because other types of volley need different technique.
causes: Poor practice habits
fixes: Practice further back around the service line with transitional volleys

good_form: On a low volley, hit it straight ahead down the line and keep the ball in front of you (hold the line).
Aim to stay in position for the next shot rather than end the point with a low volley.
Keeping the ball in front of you closes off the net and makes it easy to bisect the down-the-line and cross-court passing shots.
Treat a high ball that doesn't rise much above contact height as a high volley, not an overhead.
For a high volley, set the racket high and finish high, moving it along a bookshelf-like path.
Hold the non-hitting hand out in front to give the racket a place to go.
Hit through the high volley and send it forward so gravity brings it down into the court.
Only hit an overhead when the ball is really dropping and you have time.
Hit overheads at about half speed and place them to the side or at a slight angle.

faults.name: Low volley hit cross court
faults.looks_like: Coming forward, taking a low volley and angling it cross court, with momentum carrying you over to one side.
faults.why_it_matters: It leaves you out of position for the opponent's next shot and the low ball is hard to win with anyway.
causes: Forward momentum pulls you over even after the shot and takes time to recover from.
Trying to win the point with a low volley, which has to travel upward to clear the net.
fixes: Hit low volleys straight ahead down the line.
Keep the ball in front of you (hold the line).
Kick the can down the road and stay in position for the next shot.
outcome_effects: The opponent runs the ball down and passes you down the line.
The ball often goes out into the doubles alley, because the court is shorter and the angle sharp.

faults.name: Choosing an overhead on a high volley
faults.looks_like: Treating any ball up high as an overhead, then scrunching the arm because the ball wasn't high enough.
faults.why_it_matters: The ball needs to be really dropping to give you time for an overhead, so the wrong choice cramps the swing.
causes: Players think of only low and medium volleys, and call anything high an overhead.
The ball is high but doesn't get much higher than the contact point.
fixes: Recognize it as a high volley when the ball is high but not rising much higher than contact.
Set the racket high and finish high, like moving along a bookshelf.
Put the non-hitting hand out in front as a guide for the racket.

faults.name: Non-hitting hand down on high volley
faults.looks_like: The non-hitting hand is held low, so the racket finds that hand and gets pulled downward.
faults.why_it_matters: It stops you from hitting through the high volley.
causes: Arms tend to find each other, so the racket goes toward the other hand.
fixes: Hold the non-hitting hand up and out in front so the racket moves forward through the shot.
outcome_effects: The racket is forced downward instead of through the ball.

faults.name: Hitting overheads too hard
faults.looks_like: Blasting the overhead at full power.
faults.why_it_matters: Placement alone wins the point, and trying for speed hurts percentage and consistency.
causes: Wanting the overhead to be very fast, like 100 mph.
fixes: Cut overhead speed to about half.
Place the shot off to the side with a slight angle.

good_form: Use a continental grip for slice volleys, adjusting slightly (a bit less continental) toward the weaker side so the wrist feels better, compromising between forehand and backhand.
Keep the grip loose, loose enough that the racket could be pulled from your hand, so the wrist can absorb the ball.
On contact let the racket head go back a little to absorb pace while the grip/handle stays in place for accuracy.
Keep the racket fairly perpendicular to the ground and push through the ball for depth and penetration; slice by going under the ball only at the end while still pushing.
In ready position keep the elbows in front of the body, as if resting on a table, and rotate around elbows and wrist instead of the shoulder.
Keep the back straight and perpendicular to the ground, sit on the balls of the feet, with a slight knee bend to engage the legs.
Split step as the ball comes, and stay upright going forward; release your body weight forward only at contact.
Once you identify forehand or backhand, turn the upper body (not the whole body) to face the ball, make contact, then step.
Take two steps per volley (left then right, or step out and step in), then recover to ready position.
Keep elbows in front while stepping in; take only a small backswing if time allows, kept in front of the shoulders.

Engage the pectorals: on the forehand volley the racket arm gives power while the non-racket hand gives control and direction; on the backhand the chest opens and the non-racket arm acts as the brakes.
If the ball is far, take a few steps forward with a straight back and step in at contact instead of reaching.
On half volleys, don't slice; block and drag the ball low over the net, aiming at the net tape.
On half volleys, split step, get down to ball level, push with racket and legs as follow-through, and keep moving forward toward the net.
On half volleys, back up to give yourself time then step in; target the opponent's feet.

faults.name: Gripping the racket too tight
faults.looks_like: Tense, tight grip with tension travelling up the elbow, shoulder and neck.
faults.why_it_matters: The wrist can't absorb the ball and you can't maneuver or keep the racket moving.
causes: Concentrating on the task makes everything tense up
fixes: Hold the racket loosely, so it could be pulled from your hand
Feed-ball drill: loosen the grip and absorb power with the racket head
outcome_effects: Loss of maneuverability at the end of the stroke

faults.name: Slicing too early
faults.looks_like: Cutting down on the ball right away instead of keeping the racket perpendicular to the ground.
faults.why_it_matters: The ball doesn't penetrate, giving less depth and punch and not pushing the opponent back.
causes: Thinking that because it's a slice volley you must cut immediately
fixes: Keep the racket perpendicular and push through the ball
Go under the ball only at the end, while continuing to push

faults.name: Rotating around the shoulder / elbows not in front
faults.looks_like: Elbows not held in front of the body so the swing pivots from the shoulder.
faults.why_it_matters: It leads to late contact, too much power and poor accuracy.
causes: Elbows not set in front in the ready position
fixes: Imagine setting elbows on a table in front of you
Rotate around elbows and wrist
Keep elbows in front during drills, including when stepping in

faults.name: Leaning forward too soon
faults.looks_like: Leaning the upper body forward before contact, reaching for the ball and ending up on the toes.
faults.why_it_matters: It wastes momentum and unbalances you.
causes: Reaching with the upper body instead of taking steps
fixes: Keep the back straight and perpendicular while approaching
Take one or two steps and release weight forward only at contact

faults.name: Racket moving back as legs move forward
faults.looks_like: Legs step forward while the racket travels backward.
faults.why_it_matters: You end up hitting the ball late.
causes: Elbows not staying in front while stepping in
fixes: Keep elbows in front and step in as they stay there

faults.name: Turning the whole body / big backswing
faults.looks_like: Rotating the whole body from the legs, or taking the backswing past the shoulders.
faults.why_it_matters: It makes you hit the ball late and gets you in trouble.
causes: Backswing involving the lower body rather than just upper body
fixes: Turn only from the waist up and let the legs carry you
Use a small backswing in front, not past the shoulders, with wrist, elbow and a bit of shoulder

faults.name: Slicing the half volley / stopping at contact
faults.looks_like: Trying to slice the half volley too much and stepping or stopping where you hit instead of continuing forward.
faults.why_it_matters: The ball must stay low and you need to keep advancing to the net.
causes: Looking for slice too much
Leaning or being unbalanced
fixes: Keep the racket perpendicular and push through with legs as follow-through
Aim for the net tape and keep running forward
Keep the back straight and drop to ball level
outcome_effects: Harder to come out of the stroke and keep moving to the net
